title: Jannes and Jambres
lead: Jannes and Jambres are the names Jewish tradition gave to Pharaoh's magicians, who copied Moses' first signs (Exodus 7-8). The Old Testament does not name them; 2 Timothy 3:8 does, drawing on a tradition also found in the Damascus Document, the Targum and the Talmud.

sections.b: The Damascus Document from the Qumran sect says that when Moses and Aaron arose, Belial "raised up Yannes and his brother" (CD 5:17-19, in E. Cook's translation; Davies' translation reads "Yohanah"). The Aramaic paraphrase Targum Pseudo-Jonathan names Jannes and Jambres as Pharaoh's chief magicians who interpreted his dream before Moses' birth (on Exodus 1:15), as the magicians of Exodus 7:11, and as Balaam's two young servants (on Numbers 22:22). The Babylonian Talmud has "Yohana and Mamre" mocking Moses (Menachot 85a).

sections.h: The book of Jannes and Jambres
sections.b: Origen, in the 200s, says that there was an apocryphal book called The Book of Jannes and Jambres. Greek fragments of it survive in the Chester Beatty Papyri (no. XVI), edited and translated by Albert Pietersma, and an Ethiopic fragment was found in 2014. It is not Scripture in any church. As a source it tells us what Jewish storytellers said about Pharaoh's magicians; it gives no independent knowledge of the people behind Exodus 7. Whether 2 Timothy drew on this book or on the wider tradition of the names cannot be known from the letter.
The Roman writer Pliny the Elder (AD 77) names Jannes, with Moses, as a founder of a school of magic among the Jews (Natural History 30.2), which shows how widely the name was known.
